economics.price-define1.0004.all: Any place or arrangement where buyers and sellers come together to exchange goods or services.

economics.price-define2.0002.all: When quantity demanded is greater than quantity supplied at a given price, i.e. at a price below equilibrium; creates a shortage.

economics.price-diagram.0014.all: Demand shifts left (D1); new lower equilibrium price P1 and lower quantity Q1.

economics.price-evaluate-1.0004.all: Plan: supply fall (poor harvests) + demand rise -> higher price. Stay high if harvests stay poor (weather, disease, long time for new trees), demand keeps growing with incomes. Evaluate: harvests may recover, high price encourages new planting/entry, substitutes and falling demand at high price; depends on PED/PES and time period.

economics.price-evaluate-2.0003.all: Plan: demand rising (migration), supply inelastic (scarce land, high costs) -> rents rise. Keep rising if migration continues and supply stays inelastic. Evaluate: high rents encourage building over time, government housing/rent controls, people move elsewhere/commute, economic slowdown reduces demand.

economics.price-evaluate-3.0004.all: Plan: excess demand at OMR 450 (stock-out, resale near double) suggests price below equilibrium; raising price increases revenue/profit and rations demand. Evaluate: may harm reputation/goodwill, competitors, demand may be a launch surge; alternatively raise supply; depends on PED and long-term strategy.

economics.price-explain.0017.all: Demand for hotel rooms rises (shift right) while supply fixed/perfectly inelastic in short run; creates excess demand at old price, so price rises to new higher equilibrium; whole rise shows up as price, not quantity.

economics.price-mcq-auth.0004.all: a higher equilibrium price and quantity

economics.price-mcq-def.0001.all: The price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied

economics.production-analyse-1.0005.all: Rising incomes -> demand for services (income-elastic) increases; mechanisation/higher productivity in agriculture frees labour; competition from cheaper manufacturing abroad / deindustrialisation; growth of tourism/finance; education/skills shift.

economics.production-analyse-2.0004.all: Adding value -> higher export earnings, improves current account; job creation and multiplier effect; less reliance on volatile raw commodity prices; FDI brings technology/skills; tax revenue and economic growth.

economics.production-define1.0007.all: The difference between the price of a finished product and the cost of the inputs used to make it.

economics.production-define2.0002.all: The part of the economy that extracts or harvests natural resources, e.g. farming, fishing, mining.

economics.production-describe.0015.all: To add value to raw materials such as cotton by processing into textiles, earning more export revenue / creating jobs.

economics.production-explain.0010.all: Deindustrialisation: competition from lower-cost manufacturers abroad made factories uncompetitive so they closed; rising incomes increased demand for services, so employment shifted to tertiary sector.

economics.production-mcq-class.0020.all: Selling petrol at a filling station

economics.production-mcq-def.0006.all: The decline of the secondary/manufacturing sector as a share of an economy's output and employment

economics.production-state.0007.all: Bread (wheat farmed, flour/bread baked, sold in shop).

economics.productivity-analyse-1.0007.all: Workers specialise and become skilled/faster -> higher output per worker; lower unit costs -> competitive prices/higher profit; less time lost switching tasks; easier to use specialist machinery; quicker training.

economics.productivity-analyse-2.0006.all: Higher unit labour costs -> lower profit margins; less price competitive vs neighbouring firms, lose sales/exports; less able to invest, cycle of old machinery; may lose market share or close.

economics.productivity-assess-1.0004.all: Benefits: higher productivity, lower unit costs, speed, skill. Costs: boredom/low motivation, absenteeism, lack of flexibility, one stoppage halts line, dependence. Judgement: depends on job rotation, wages, automation.

economics.productivity-assess-2.0006.all: Options: subsidise training/education, investment allowances/subsidies for new machinery, improve infrastructure, R&D. Evaluate: cost/opportunity cost to government, time lags, firms may not take it up, depends on quality.

economics.productivity-define1.0003.all: Where the production process is broken down into separate tasks, with workers specialising in a particular task.

economics.productivity-define2.0001.all: A measure of output per unit of input (e.g. per worker per hour); how efficiently factors of production are used.

economics.productivity-describe.0010.all: Lower costs per unit allow firms to cut prices, so consumers get cheaper goods / higher real incomes.

economics.production-define2.0002.problem: Second mark is awarded for examples (farming, fishing, mining) but the guidance says do not award marks for examples.
economics.production-define2.0002.fix: Second mark for a developed element, e.g. 'extraction of raw materials / natural resources from land or sea (1), producing raw materials for other sectors (1)'; or remove the 'no marks for examples' note.

economics.productivity-define2.0001.problem: Second mark is for an example (output per worker per hour) while the guidance says do not award marks for examples.
economics.productivity-define2.0001.fix: Output per unit of input (1), a measure of how efficiently factors of production are used (1); or drop the 'no marks for examples' note.
